questions.q: In the model ADR, why did the team choose a static threshold (Option A) over a learned classifier (Option B) for now?
options: Static thresholds are always technically superior to learned classifiers in every situation
The decision had nothing to do with data availability
They currently lack the labeled 'was this answer correct' data needed to train or validate a classifier reliably, and the static-threshold period itself would generate that data for a future Option B
Learned classifiers are impossible to build for any confidence-routing problem
questions.explain: The Context section explicitly names the missing labeled dataset as the deciding factor, and the Decision section turns the static-threshold period into a way to generate that very data for later.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the static threshold is 'real preparation for Option B rather than a dead end'?
options: The static threshold permanently replaces any need for a learned classifier
Static thresholds and learned classifiers have no real relationship to each other
The static threshold period produces no useful byproduct at all
The outcomes recorded during the static-threshold period become exactly the labeled data a future learned classifier would need to be trained and validated
questions.explain: This is a deliberate design choice in the ADR -- the interim solution isn't just a stopgap, it actively solves the blocker (missing labeled data) that prevented the more sophisticated option from being viable in the first place.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say proposing a learned classifier from day one could still be a legitimate, defensible answer, even though it differs from the model ADR's conclusion?
options: Any answer is equally correct regardless of the reasoning behind it
The model ADR's conclusion is simply wrong and should always be overridden
This exercise has no single defensible reasoning process at all

If a student reasonably assumed Northbeam already had sufficient labeled historical data (a detail the scenario didn't fully specify), that assumption changes which option the SAME reasoning framework would support
questions.explain: The point of the exercise is reasoning the same way the model answer reasons (naming real trade-offs, being honest about what's known/unknown) -- a different but well-justified assumption can legitimately lead to a different, equally defensible conclusion.

questions.q: What does this capstone say is the actual point of the exercise, as distinct from matching the model ADR's exact conclusion?
options: Avoiding any reference to cost, latency, or team expertise in the written decision
Reasoning the way the model answer reasons -- naming real trade-offs honestly, being explicit about what's unknown, and writing the decision down so it can be understood and challenged later
Always agreeing with whatever conclusion a model answer reaches, regardless of the scenario's actual details
Memorizing the model ADR's exact wording for future use
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that matching the model answer's REASONING process matters more than matching its exact conclusion -- a different, well-justified conclusion given different assumptions is still a success.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'walk me through how you'd decide X' is such a common Staff/Principal interview format?
options: It only tests a candidate's knowledge of one specific vector database product
It is primarily a test of how fast a candidate can talk

It tests whether a candidate can structure an ambiguous decision, name real trade-offs honestly, and communicate reasoning clearly -- everything this course covered -- not just whether they land on a specific answer
This interview format has no real connection to any Staff/Principal-level skill
questions.explain: This format exercises the full skill set the course built: structuring ambiguity, honest trade-off analysis, and clear communication of the reasoning -- which is exactly why it's used so often at this level.
